projects.title: HU-001C Handheld Game Machine
projects.summary: An '80s-style handheld game machine, soldered, assembled, and debugged from a kit.
projects.description: A DIY handheld gaming system built from the HU-001C Funny Game Machine kit. A programmed STC15F2K60S2 microcontroller reads five push buttons and drives an LED dot-matrix display, a three-digit numeric display, and a buzzer to run several retro-style games. Members identified parts, read the supplied circuit references, soldered the board, fit the clear case, and tested the finished system. The club assembled and tested an existing kit; PCB design and game firmware were outside this build's scope.
build: Identify components and check resistor value, IC socket notch, transistor orientation, and capacitor polarity
Assemble the battery holder and connect power leads with correct polarity
Solder the core components, then the buttons, buzzer, matrix sections, and numeric display
Solder the micro-USB connector and IC socket, then seat the microcontroller and button caps
Close the clear case, install batteries, and test controls, display, game switching, and sound
troubleshooting: Excess solder risking bridges: reheated, desoldered, and re-soldered with less
Incomplete through-hole joints: reflowed, reworking from the other side where needed
Battery pack initially missed: added afterward, matching polarity to PCB markings
Intermittent power: battery contact clips extended slightly for firmer contact

projects.title: Light-Activated LED & Buzzer Alarm
projects.summary: A 3 V light-sensing alarm that lights an LED and sounds a buzzer, with adjustable sensitivity.
projects.description: A 3 V light-activated alarm that detects changes in ambient light and responds with an LED and a buzzer. A 5516 photoresistor and 10 kΩ potentiometer set the bias on an 8050 NPN transistor; when light crosses the chosen threshold, Q1 pulls its collector low, lighting the LED and switching an 8550 PNP high-side transistor to sound the buzzer. Members went from a printed schematic and parts kit to a soldered, working PCB.
build: Match each component to its PCB reference designator and verify values and orientation
Solder resistors and low-profile parts first
Install the LDR, potentiometer, LED, transistors, buzzer, and battery leads
Inspect for cold joints, bridges, and reversed polarized parts, then trim leads
Final visual inspection before connecting the 3 V supply
troubleshooting: LED dimmer than expected: continuity-checked the whole PCB with a Fluke 17B
Several beginner solder joints reflowed and verified
Circuit worked after repairs; remaining dim LED identified as a likely defective part and kept as a teaching example
